The Danube River. Europe's second-longest river, flowing seventeen seventy-one miles from Germany's Black Forest through ten countries to the Black Sea. It is the continent's most internationally important waterway, connecting central Europe to the Balkans and the east.

The Danube originates in Germany's Black Forest mountains and flows southeast, forming the border between several nations, including Hungary and Slovakia, and later Serbia and Romania. For the Romans, the Danube served as the empire's northern frontier. The Danube limes, a fortified border, marked the Roman Empire's limit against Germanic and later nomadic tribes. The most dramatic section is the Danube gorge between Serbia and Romania, known as the Iron Gate. This is one of Europe's most striking landscapes and was historically a major transportation bottleneck.

Vienna, Budapest, and Belgrade are the great cities built on the Danube's banks. Medieval and early modern central European power depended entirely on control of the Danube. The Danube delta in Romania is Europe's second-largest river delta, a vast wetland sanctuary for migratory birds and extraordinary biodiversity.

Today the river is subject to international water management. The 1948 Danube Convention and later treaties govern riparian rights and navigation among upstream and downstream nations. The river's strategic importance has linked it to the history of Germany and Austria, whose founding and power relied on Danube commerce. Hungary's Budapest and the Danube valley remain inseparable from Hungarian history. The Ottoman Empire controlled significant Danube territory for centuries, and Danube crossings were sites of major Ottoman wars. The river separates and connects the Balkan peninsula to central Europe.
